opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core problem with benchmaxxing is that a benchmark is only ever a proxy for what we actually care about. When you start optimizing directly for the number, you tend to get really good at the specific quirks of that test without getting meaningfully better at the underlying capability. It's Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

In practice, that looks like a few things. You might overfit to the format of the questions, or to a narrow distribution of tasks that doesn't reflect how people actually use the model. Sometimes there's subtle contamination, where test-like data leaks into training, and suddenly the score jumps but the model hasn't really learned anything new. And then you ship something that looks great on a leaderboard but feels disappointing when someone sits down and tries to get real work done with it.

The bigger cost is that it distorts where you spend your effort. Research time is finite. If teams are chasing a point or two on a saturated benchmark, they're not working on the harder, messier problems that matter for users, or for things like safety and reliability, which are often harder to measure cleanly.

So my view is that evals should be a tool for understanding the model, not the goal itself. The way I think about building good evaluations is to make them as close as possible to real-world, economically valuable tasks, keep refreshing them so they don't go stale, and always pair the numbers with qualitative judgment, actually looking at outputs and talking to people who use the models. If the benchmark goes up and real-world usefulness doesn't, that's a signal the benchmark has stopped telling you the truth.

r001.rationale: The response says teams optimize for benchmark scores and test quirks without improving underlying capability, while real-world usefulness may not improve.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so benchmaxxing is basically when you optimize a model to score well on a specific benchmark rather than to actually be good at the underlying capability the benchmark was supposed to measure. And the reason I think it's bad is that benchmarks are proxies. Every eval we build is an imperfect, compressed stand-in for something we really care about, like "can this model do real scientific research" or "can it be a useful software engineer." The moment you start training against the proxy directly, the proxy stops telling you anything about the real thing. It's Goodhart's law, basically.

The thing that worries me most is that it corrupts your own signal. A lot of people frame this as a marketing problem, like, oh, companies are gaming leaderboards. And sure, that happens. But the deeper cost is internal. If your eval numbers go up but the model isn't actually more capable, you've lost your ability to make good decisions about what to work on next. You think you solved something and you didn't. And you often don't find out until the model is in users' hands and it falls over on things that look nothing like the test set.

There's also a contamination angle. Once a benchmark is widely used, the questions, the solutions, the discussion of them end up on the internet, and then in pretraining data. So a model can "know" the answers without having the skill. If you then also fine-tune on things that look like the benchmark, you're compounding it. The number keeps climbing and it means less and less.

What I'd rather see, and what we try to do, is treat evals as measurement instruments, not training targets. Keep held-out sets that nobody trains on. Design tasks that are as close as possible to real-world work, with real experts grading them, so the gap between the proxy and the thing you care about is small. And when a benchmark saturates, build a harder one instead of squeezing the last two points out of the old one. The goal is a model that's genuinely more useful, and benchmarks should be how we check that, not the thing we're building toward.

r001.rationale: The response defines BenchMaxxing as optimizing benchmark scores instead of the underlying capability, and contrasts that with real-world tasks and a model that is genuinely useful.

astra-6.text:
I think the danger is that the benchmark becomes the goal, rather than a way to measure progress. You can spend a lot of effort getting a model to score higher on a particular set of questions without making it more useful or reliable in the situations people actually care about.

Benchmarks are useful—you need ways to compare models and understand whether a change helped. But if you optimize too narrowly for them, you can miss weaknesses that the benchmark doesn’t capture. I’d want to see whether those gains carry over to unfamiliar problems and real tasks. The score should be evidence of improvement, not the definition of improvement.

r001.rationale: The response says optimizing narrowly to raise benchmark scores can fail to improve usefulness or reliability in the situations people care about, distinguishing benchmark performance from real-task usefulness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the problem is when the benchmark becomes the goal, rather than a way to measure progress. You can get very good at the particular tasks a benchmark rewards without making the model more useful or reliable in practice.

Benchmarks are valuable—you need ways to compare models and understand whether a change helped. But if every development decision is driven by a leaderboard score, you risk missing weaknesses that the benchmark doesn’t capture. You also lose some of the signal from that benchmark as you repeatedly optimize against it.

What I’d want is evidence that the improvement generalizes: does it hold up on fresh tasks, in different settings, and on things users actually care about? The score should support that judgment, rather than replace it.

r001.rationale: It describes optimizing development decisions for benchmark or leaderboard scores at the expense of practical usefulness, and contrasts those scores with tasks users actually care about.
